sections.title: Opening Scene (Creative Reconstruction — Clearly Labeled Fiction Where Facts Are Unknown)
sections.body:
[Note: this is an authored, imaginative reconstruction built only on the one confirmed fact — Sunday pancakes with Aunt. Every sensory or anecdotal detail below is invented and marked as such. Keep what feels true; replace or delete the rest with real details as they surface.]

Sunday mornings had their own clock. Not the alarm — something softer. The tick of a heating pan, a cupboard opening, the particular quiet of a kitchen before the household wakes.

The batter was always the first thing. Aunt's hand tipped the jug, flour fell in a slow white curtain, and I remember (or invent — I can no longer tell) her saying we were watching for the right bubbles. Not too many. Not too few. Sunday pancakes, she may have said, are the only recipe measured by patience.

The stove did what stoves do. The first pancake often went wrong; I believe that was treated as ordinary, almost a rule of its own. Then the rest of the stack, warm, slightly uneven, and a plate that seemed small to begin with and never emptied.

What I actually have is the knowing: that Sunday meant pancakes, and pancakes meant Aunt. Everything else — the room, the weather, what we talked about or didn't — is a frame I am still building around that one bright fact.

sections.title: Memory-Anchoring Method: Growing the Story From One Fact

items.text: Write one sentence per sense about the pancake memory: what it looked like, smelled, sounded, tasted, felt. Mark each as 'remembered' or 'guessed.'
List every other person, place or object that touches the pancake memory (the pan, the plate, the kitchen, whoever else was awake). Each one is a doorway to a second memory.
Open a capture file today: date, prompt word, then five minutes of free writing per prompt — no editing, no judging whether it is true.
Use a rotating object sequence — kitchen, house, neighborhood, school, work, travel — writing whatever surfaces, even fragments.
At each session's end, add one line stating which details you would want to verify with someone, and who might know.

sections.title: Before the Next Draft
items: What is the one thing you most want a reader to feel by the end of the pancake scene?
Who, if anyone, could confirm or correct one practical detail about the pancake memory — and might you ask them?
Should recurring anchors like 'the knowing' be kept as the story's voice between scenes?

sections.body:
[This is authored imaginative prose, not a record of your memory. The only facts used are the two you confirmed: Sunday, and pancakes with Aunt. Everything else — the kitchen, who cooked, how it tasted, what was said, whether it happened once or many times — is written as deliberately blank and may be replaced with real detail as it surfaces.]

Sunday. Pancakes. Aunt.

I could begin anywhere, and everything else is still dark. Was there a kitchen, and whose? Did the light come in, or was it a gray morning? I do not know. I know only that the day was Sunday and that pancakes were there, and that Aunt was there with them.

So I will let this first page be spare. A day named. A food. A person. Three facts standing in a row, and around them a silence I am not yet able to fill without making things up.

Who poured the batter — I do not know. Who turned the pancakes, who set them down — I do not know. Whether Aunt spoke, or was quiet, or handed me a plate — unknown. Whether this happened every Sunday or one Sunday — unknown. Whether I was small — unknown. Whether I liked them — unknown. I will not guess.

The rest of my life can wait. This chapter begins where the record begins: a Sunday, pancakes, and Aunt. The blanks are not failures. They are the shape of what I am still learning to remember.

sections.body: When a detail returns on its own, write it in one sentence and mark where it came from (your own recall, a photo, a letter, a relative's account). Keep every category you are unsure of explicitly open: setting, who made the pancakes, the recipe, other people present, feelings, dates, and any recurring pattern. If you later interview someone, treat their account as their memory, not as yours, and label it that way in the manuscript. The chapter can grow by adding one verified line at a time rather than filling the blanks by speculation.
